newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish unions, big employers welcome 1997 budget.
newsitem.headline: Irish unions, big employers welcome 1997 budget.

text.p: Ireland's big employers and unions welcomed Finance Minister Ruairi Quinn's 1997 Irish budget, describing it as a basis for progress, but small firms complained there were no new special measures for them.
Quinn delivered his third budget on Wednesday, announcing the biggest tax reduction package in Irish history in an election year budget.
He cut the standard income tax to 26 percent from 27 percent, trimmed pay-related social insurance (PSRI)-- a payroll tax -- by a percentage point and widened personal tax bands.
The Irish Business and Employers' Confederation said the tax reductions were "welcome and significant".

"The income tax reform in this budget, both in its structure and scale significantly improves the incentive for work, relieves pressure on wages and should therefore give some relief to those businesses most exposed to competition."
It said a cut in corporation tax, to 36 percent from 38 percent, was a welcome delivery on Quinn's 1995 commitment to make on-going progress in this area.
But the lobby group, which represents some 4,000 companies in all sectors, said the estimated growth in public spending in 1997 was unwarranted.

"IBEC attaches a very high priority to the minister's stated commitment to multi-annual budgeting, which must prioritise much slower growth in spending and urges strong political and administrative commitment to a vigorous modernisation programme in the public service."
The Irish Congress of Trade Unions, the umbrella body for Irish unions, said the budget had taken the first steps toward sharing the benefits of economic growth fairly.
"We still have a long way to go to achieve fairness for all but this budget marks an important first step on that road," ICTU said in a statement.

"While more radical tax reform is required and long term unemployment remains a major challenge, it would be small-minded not to acknowledge that today's budget does attempt to share the benefits fairly," it said.
Ireland's largest union SIPTU also approved.

"Having examined the budget against the objectives contained in "Partnership 2000', we are satisfied that the commitments entered into by the government in these negotiations have been delivered on and therefore we welcome this budget," it said.

Partnership 2000, the wage agreement drawn up by government, employers and unions late last year, promises tax reductions of one billion punts on a full-year cost basis over the life of the agreement.
But the Irish Small Firms Association (SFA) said the budget was not for small business.

"Minister Quinn said he recognised the important role of small business in our growing economy and job creation. Yet small business gets no new special measures in today's announcement," it said in a statement.
